From Section 9.5 we know that the average kinetic energy of a molecule in the gas is (3>2)kBT, which is (1>2)kBT for each of the x, y, and z directions of motion. Therefore, we interpret kBT as a measure of the average energy available to each molecule in a gas at tem- perature T. So, the ratio hn>kBT determines whether there is sufficient energy in the gas to put the molecules into excited states. At 300 K, the value of kBT is 4.14 × 10221 J, which is a factor of 10 smaller than the vibrational quantum of CO. Insert- ing these numbers into Equation 12.22 gives the relative probability as 3.03 × 1025. This means that only 3 molecules in a group of 100,000 are in the first ex- cited state at 300 K. At 1000 K, the value of kBT is 1.38 × 10220 J, which is closer to the value of the CO vibrational quantum and gives a relative population of 4.41 × 1022. This case study shows that CO molecules do not have significant vibrational en- ergy unless the temperature is quite high. This happens because CO has a triple bond and, therefore, a large force constant (k 5 1902 N m21). The correlation between force constant and bond order in diatomic molecules is explained by molecular or- bital theory, and is summarized in Figure 6.20. Other diatomic molecules will have quantitatively different distributions, as determined by their structure.
